prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators remain my preferred single achievement. The Kane-Mele Z2 classification identified a simple, robust mechanism: time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling protect edge or surface states, and the topological invariant is a property of the bulk band structure that does not depend on microscopic details. That is the kind of universal mechanism I look for. It was followed by a concrete experimental confirmation (Molenkamp's HgTe quantum wells, 2007) and by more than fifteen years of independent transport and ARPES confirmation across many materials, so the interpretation is stable. Four members ranked it in their top three, including Eriksson who put it first, and the theory-plus-experiment trio Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the configuration three of the four supporters proposed. The idea changed how materials are classified, which makes it a physics prize and not a technology prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit and overlap. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal for HgTe, which made the experiment possible, is outside the credited names (and Zhang is deceased), the 3D case (Hasan, Moore, Balents, Fu) is split off, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases of matter, so a second topology prize needs a clear argument that this is a distinct discovery. By comparison B022 has far broader opening support (three first places, six top-three rankings) and a cleaner two-person attribution. If the committee weighs a clean, uncontested allocation above field-level influence, B022 is the safer prize. My own opening first choice, B027, has only my support and a contested priority history, so I do not put it forward as the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Topological insulators are a quantitatively computable new state of matter with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a coherent trio; he also notes that real graphene has too small a spin-orbit gap to realise the original Kane-Mele phase.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on the maturity. Your graphene point matters for the citation: the priority of Kane and Mele rests on the Z2 concept and the invariant, not on graphene as a material, so the citation should name the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators in general and should not say graphene. I would also press the question you leave open, whether the 2016 prize leaves enough room. My answer is that the 2016 prize was about topological defects and phase transitions in model systems, whereas this one is about symmetry-protected band topology in real materials. I find that distinction defensible, but not self-evident.

responses.point: She proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, pairing the theory with the two original experiments (2D transport and 3D ARPES), and leaves out Mele.
responses.response: I disagree with dropping Mele. Kane and Mele published the Z2 quantum spin Hall proposal together and the invariant is theirs jointly, so omitting one of them would be hard to justify scientifically. Including Hasan would mean choosing between 3D ARPES credit and Molenkamp's 2D observation, which is the experiment that tested the Kane-Mele and BHZ prediction directly, and the same contested 3D credit (Moore, Balents, Fu) would then be reopened. With a three-person limit I would keep the 2D theory-experiment pair and acknowledge the 3D work in the citation text or in the committee's background material. If the committee prefers to honour the 3D experiments, I would want to see how it handles Fu, Moore and Balents.

responses.point: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a new measurement technique that reaches 1e-18 uncertainty, with Katori as proposer and Ye as the performance driver, a natural two-person prize.
responses.response: I accept the attribution argument: Katori and Ye is the cleanest configuration on the list, and the independent clock comparisons are the right kind of evidence. Where I differ is on what counts as the discovery. This is a precision instrument advance whose physics (magic-wavelength trapping, Lamb-Dicke confinement) is an application of known atomic physics, and it overlaps with the 2005 comb prize and Wineland's 2012 prize. I do not think it is unworthy, and I list it as my first alternative, but I would put the conceptual novelty of an invariant that classifies matter above a smaller uncertainty budget.

responses.point: Baryon acoustic oscillations are a clean standard ruler detected in SDSS and 2dFGRS and now central to dark-energy constraints; he ranked it first.
responses.response: The physics is attractive and the DESI results raise its relevance, but I am concerned about who the discovery belongs to. The acoustic-peak physics was worked out by Peebles and Yu and by Sunyaev and Zeldovich, the 2005 detections were collaboration results, and you note yourself that earlier cosmology prizes (2006, 2011, 2019) may weigh against repetition. Only three members ranked it, and it is outside my expertise in the observational details, so I would be glad to hear whether the committee believes a three-person attribution is defensible here. For now, I have not moved it into my configuration.

responses.point: Circuit QED made a superconducting artificial atom strongly coupled to a single microwave photon on a chip and underpins superconducting processors; he also flags his own possible conflict of interest.
responses.response: I appreciate that you disclosed your field proximity, and I agree the discovery is original and well reproduced. My reservation is the one you name yourself: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is very recent, and the transmon, Girvin's theory and Devoret's role sit partly outside the credited trio. A second circuit prize within a year seems hard to justify unless the committee can state clearly what the light-matter discovery adds beyond that.

uncertainties: Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves enough room for a distinct prize on Z2 topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect.
Whether the 3D topological insulator experiments (Hasan, with Moore, Balents and Fu on theory) must be recognised alongside the 2D HgTe observation, which the three-person limit would not allow.
How the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal for HgTe should be handled in the citation and in the committee's report.
B004 is listed separately in the longlist, but I regard it as the same discovery as B045. I am relying on memory of the credit history and have not verified it.
Whether B022 should simply be preferred because of its much broader opening support and its cleaner attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I note that I work at the University of Gothenburg, in the same physics environment as colleagues Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers, and that Johansson has himself flagged a possible conflict on B039 and B032. I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate.
